title: An 8-week resistance training protocol for quadriceps adaptation
author: Pietro Mannarino
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.ykwfuxe

respectively. To our knowledge, only Hsiao et al. (2015) have
previously addressed this question. Examining the proximal
PT in a reduced sample composed of ﬁve subjects in two dif-
ferent days with a 1-week interval, they found an intra-rater
ICC value ranging from 0 /C1742 to 0 /C1874. Our reproducibility
values were relatively lower and comparing both protocols,
one important factor could be identiﬁed. Their group included
a 2-h rest recommendation before the examination. Although
our exams were performed in the morning period and sub-
jects reported no previous physical activity in that day, no
additional control was made for daily activities as walking
long distances or going up or down stairs. This could acutely
change PT properties in different days, what would impair
reproducibility. Further investigation controlling these param-
eters and analysing ICC with well-deﬁned pre-examination
protocols should be tested.
We recognize some study limitations. First, we used a con-
venience sample composed of healthy young male volunteers
from the staff of our institution, so these ﬁndings cannot be
generalized to females, other age range or a speciﬁc athletic
population. Potential confounding factors such as smoking
and nutrition were not accounted for, although all the partici-
pants were free of systemic or local disease. The leg prefer-
ence in the present study was self-reported, and no
experimental assessment of hand or leg preference was per-
formed. At last, this was a cross-sectional observational study;
no causal effects could be analysed. Additional longitudinal
trials are warranted for further clariﬁcation of the effect of
quadriceps function on PT properties. Furthermore, long-term
interventions protocols should provide an insight into how
tendon adapts when examined in the light of SSI.
Conclusion
The present study revealed no signiﬁcant differences in PT E
and KT between legs, suggesting that in similar loading envi-
ronments, side dominance does not affect these parameters.
No signiﬁcant correlations were found between KT and PT E,
suggesting that quadriceps strength is not predictor for PT
mechanical properties in subjects with no speciﬁc training
engagement. ICC values from SSI were higher for measures
taken in the same day when compared to measures taken in
different days. Further investigation on SSI acquisition proto-
cols should be conducted to guarantee higher inter-day ICC
values and greater SSI reliability.

steps.title: Obtain ethics approval and consent
steps.instruction: Secure approval from the University Hospital Ethics Committee (registration numbers 570.945 and 519.230) and obtain written informed consent from each participant before any testing.

steps.title: Recruit and screen participants
steps.instruction: Select 23 volunteer medical‑staff members, male, aged 25–30 years, right‑handed and right‑leg dominant; exclude anyone with a history of knee pain/injury, systemic disease, or prior knee surgery. After exclusion of one subject with persistent knee pain, retain 22 participants.

steps.title: Record anthropometric data
steps.instruction: Measure and record each subject’s body weight, height, age, and dominant leg.

steps.title: Prepare subject for patellar‑tendon ultrasound
steps.instruction: Have the subject lie supine with the knee flexed to 30° and supported by a custom knee‑and‑ankle stabilizer that keeps the leg in neutral coronal and transverse alignment. Allow a 10‑minute rest in this position, and keep the room temperature at 20 °C.

substeps.instruction: Apply a generous amount of coupling gel to the inferior pole of the patella.
Position an Aixplorer ultrasound system (v9, Supersonic Imaging, Aix‑en‑Provence, France) with a 60‑mm linear‑array transducer set to 4–15 MHz.
Align the transducer with the patellar tendon longitudinally using B‑mode imaging.
Activate shear‑wave elastography mode once a clear tendon image is obtained.
Hold the transducer stationary for 5 seconds to acquire an SSI map.
Capture two images per knee for offline analysis.
Define a rectangular region of interest (ROI) 5–20 mm distal to the inferior patellar pole, excluding the paratenon.
Use the ‘Q‑box tracing™’ tool to obtain Young’s modulus (E) values; repeat the measurement twice per tendon and record the mean E.

steps.title: Measure maximal isometric knee extension torque
steps.instruction: Using a Biodex isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex Medical Systems, Shirley, NY, USA) set at 70° knee flexion, assess each subject’s maximal voluntary isometric torque.

substeps.instruction: Seat the subject on the dynamometer chair and fasten inextensible straps around the waist, trunk, and distal thigh.
Adjust back‑rest inclination, seat translation, and dynamometer height so the rotation axis aligns with the lateral femoral condyle.
Fix the right knee to the lever arm 5 cm above the lateral malleolus.
Perform a warm‑up consisting of two submaximal isometric knee extensions.
Instruct the subject to execute two maximal voluntary isometric contractions, each lasting 5 seconds, with a 1‑minute passive rest between trials.
Provide verbal encouragement and visual torque feedback throughout.
Record the highest peak torque (gravity‑corrected) as the subject’s knee extension torque.

steps.title: Repeat measurements on a second day
steps.instruction: Conduct the entire ultrasound and torque testing protocol again after a minimum 1‑week interval, examining both knees in each session.

steps.title: Data processing and reliability analysis
steps.instruction: For each knee, calculate the mean Young’s modulus from the two SSI images per day. Compute intra‑day and inter‑day intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), coefficient of variation (CV), and perform paired t‑tests and Pearson correlations as described in the statistical analysis section.
